g11-mathematics-um8-t1.overview: The fundamental principle of counting (multiplication rule) and the addition rule: counting outcomes without listing them — the foundation of probability.
objectives: Apply the multiplication principle to sequential choices
Apply the addition principle to disjoint cases
Count with and without repetition allowed
Build counting trees for small problems
Spot when to multiply vs add
g11-mathematics-um8-t1.simple: COUNTING WITHOUT LISTING. MULTIPLICATION PRINCIPLE: if step 1 has m ways and step 2 has n ways, the pair has m·n outcomes. Menu: 3 starters × 4 mains = 12 meals. License plate: 2 letters (26 each) + 3 digits (10 each) = 26·26·10·10·10 = 676,000. 4-digit PINs: 10⁴ = 10,000; with NO repeats: 10·9·8·7 = 5040 — repetition rules change the count. WHY it multiplies: each of the m first-steps branches into n second-steps — a tree with m·n leaves. ADDITION PRINCIPLE: if A can happen in m ways OR B in n ways and the cases DON'T OVERLAP, total = m + n. 'Choose one book from 5 math or 8 physics' = 13 (either/or, disjoint). THE DECISION: AND (sequential/independent slots) → multiply; OR (mutually exclusive cases) → add. 'Committee of 1 man AND 1 woman from 5 men, 3 women' = 5·3 = 15. 'Send one person who is a mathematician OR physicist' from disjoint groups 5+3 = 8. Overlap? Add then SUBTRACT the intersection (inclusion-exclusion): |A∪B| = |A|+|B|−|A∩B|. Every permutation and combination ahead is this principle in a costume.
g11-mathematics-um8-t1.detailed:
Formal statement. If a task decomposes into k sequential subtasks with n₁, n₂, …, nₖ independent choices, total outcomes = n₁·n₂·…·nₖ (product rule). If a task has k mutually exclusive case-types with n₁, …, nₖ realizations, total = Σnᵢ (sum rule). Independence in the product rule: the number of options at each step must not depend on earlier choices — when it does, either track cases or fix the order of choices.

Repetition variants. Strings of length r from an alphabet of n: WITH repetition nʳ; WITHOUT n(n−1)…(n−r+1) (each slot loses one used symbol). Example: 3-letter codes from A–E: 5³ = 125 with reuse; 5·4·3 = 60 without.

Case-splitting. When a constraint breaks independence ('even PIN', 'starts with a vowel'), split into disjoint cases, count each by the product rule, then ADD the cases. The two rules dance together: multiply within cases, add across them.

Inclusion-exclusion (2 sets). Counting 'A or B' when both can hold: A + B double-counts A∩B — subtract it once. 'Divisible by 2 or 3 below 31': 15 + 10 − 5 (multiples of 6) = 20. This is the addition rule repaired for overlapping cases.

workedExamples.problem: Route count: Addis to Adama via 3 roads, Adama to Hawassa via 4. Trip options?
How many 3-digit numbers (100–999) have all distinct digits?
Choose a course: 6 options in Monday OR 5 in Tuesday OR 3 in Wednesday (no overlaps).
Committee: 2 teachers from 7 AND 1 student from 4?
Numbers ≤ 60 divisible by 3 OR 5?

commonMistakes: Adding when steps combine (3 roads AND 4 roads = 7 — wrong; 12)
Multiplying disjoint cases (either/or cases ADD)
Forgetting the leading-zero restriction in digit counts
Repetition assumed or denied silently — read the problem's rule
Overlapping cases multiplied instead of split-then-added
Double-counting overlaps — that's what inclusion-exclusion fixes
applications: Passwords & PINs: security = counting (10⁴ vs 5040 guesses)
Phone numbers & plates: designing enough codes for a population
Scheduling: class-period combinations, meeting slots
Game odds: dice, cards, lottery — all product-rule counts
g11-mathematics-um8-t1.summary: The fundamental counting principle: sequential independent choices MULTIPLY (m·n outcomes for m-then-n); disjoint either/or cases ADD (m + n). Repetition allowed → nʳ strings; forbidden → shrinking slots n(n−1)…. Constraints split the count into cases: multiply within, add across. Overlapping cases need inclusion-exclusion: |A| + |B| − |A∩B|. These two rules — AND ×, OR + — generate every count in this unit.

questions.q: 'Red card OR king' from 52 (overlap: red king):
The sum rule needs disjoint cases.
Without repetition, the k-th slot always has n options.
AND between independent steps means ___ the counts:
Explain why the product rule works using a tree diagram.
questions.explanation: Each of the m first-step outcomes roots its own n-branch subtree (independence guarantees every step-2 option remains available); the tree's leaves — the complete outcomes — number m·n

g11-mathematics-um8-t2.overview: Permutations (order matters) and combinations (order doesn't): nPr = n!/(n−r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!), their relationship, and choosing which counts a situation.
objectives: Compute factorials and simplify factorial ratios
Count arrangements with nPr
Count selections with nCr
Convert between them: nPr = nCr·r!
Model real situations with the right one
g11-mathematics-um8-t2.simple: ORDER decides everything. PERMUTATION = arrangement IN LINE: president, secretary, treasurer from 10 members — roles differ, so (A,B,C) ≠ (C,B,A): nPr = n!/(n−r)! = 10·9·8 = 720. Read it as the product rule: r shrinking slots. COMBINATION = SELECTION, no order: a 3-person committee from 10 — {A,B,C} is one group, but it appears as 3! = 6 permutations (all orderings of the same trio): nCr = nPr/r! = 720/6 = 120. THE TEST: 'would swapping the picks change the outcome?' Roles, rankings, digit codes, race results → PERMUTE. Teams, hands of cards, topping a pizza, handshake pairs → COMBINE. Factorial facts: n! = n(n−1)···1, 0! = 1 (the empty arrangement — one way to choose nothing). Symmetry: nCr = nC(n−r) — choosing 3 to include = choosing 7 to exclude. Pascal's triangle builds combinations row by row (each entry = sum of two above). Worked classics: handshake count at a 20-person meeting = 20C2 = 190; 5-card poker hands = 52C5 = 2,598,960.
g11-mathematics-um8-t2.detailed:
Formulas & mechanics. nPr = n!/(n−r)! — the falling product of r factors starting at n. nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!). Simplify by CANCELING before multiplying: 10C4 = (10·9·8·7)/(4·3·2·1) = 210 — never compute 10! = 3,628,800 blindly. The bridge nPr = nCr · r!: first CHOOSE the r members (unordered), then ARRANGE them (r! orders).

Recognition drills. 'First, second, third place' — ordered → permute (12P3 = 1320). 'A trio of friends' — unordered → combine (12C3 = 220). 'Numbers formed from digits' — positions are roles → permute, with the repetition rule from t1. 'Choosing 2 captains' — one pair, both equal → combine.

Restriction handling. 'Committee must include the chair': fix her, choose the rest (9C4). 'At least one girl': total − none (complement counting — the probability trick early). 'Boys together': bundle as one super-item, permute internally × arrange the bundle — the block method.

Identities worth knowing. nC0 = nCn = 1; nC1 = n; Σᵣ nCr = 2ⁿ (every subset — each element in/out: the product rule again); Pascal: nCr = n−1C(r−1) + n−1Cr (case split on whether the special element is chosen).

workedExamples.problem: 8 runners: gold, silver, bronze — how many podiums?
Same 8 runners: a 3-person doping-test group?
workedExamples.answer: 56 groups (the trio is one set — divide the 336 by 3! = 6)

workedExamples.problem: Simplify 10C4 without big numbers.
Committee of 4 from 6 men, 4 women, with at least one woman?
Arrange MISSISSIPPI.
workedExamples.answer: 34,650 distinct arrangements (divide out the identical swaps)

commonMistakes: Permuting selections (committee orderings double-count by r!)
Combining arrangements (podiums need order — dividing loses cases)
Computing full factorials instead of canceling
Forgetting 0! = 1 in formulas
'At least one' counted directly (messy) instead of by complement
Repeated items: permuting as if distinct (MISSISSIPPI needs the divide)
applications: Lotteries & draws: winning odds are combination counts
Cryptography: key-space sizes are permutation counts
Sports leagues: fixtures (pairs) vs standings (orders)
Molecular biology: DNA sequences = permutations with repetition (4ⁿ)
g11-mathematics-um8-t2.summary: Permutations count ORDERED arrangements: nPr = n!/(n−r)! — shrinking slots. Combinations count UNORDERED selections: nCr = nPr/r! = n!/(r!(n−r)!) — groups, not lines. The question 'does swapping picks change the outcome?' selects the tool. Cancel factorials early; use symmetry nCr = nC(n−r); handle 'at least one' by complement and 'together' by bundling; divide by repeats! for identical items. Σ nCr = 2ⁿ — the subset count — and Pascal's triangle is the case-split identity made visible.

questions.q: Choosing 3 of 7 for a flat team:
Sum of row n of Pascal's triangle:
How many 4-person committees from 6 boys, 5 girls with exactly 2 each?
Explain why nCr = nPr/r! with a concrete example.
questions.explanation: Each unordered trio from {A..E} (10 of them) appears in 3! = 6 orders among the 60 permutations of 3 from 5 — so permutations = combinations × orderings: 60 = 10·6; dividing removes the order-duplicates

g11-mathematics-um8-t3.overview: The Binomial Theorem: expanding (a+b)ⁿ with Pascal's coefficients — Σ nCr·aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ — general terms, specific coefficients, and the theorem's counting soul.
objectives: Expand (a+b)ⁿ using binomial coefficients
Build/read Pascal's triangle
Find any single term: T(r+1) = nCr·aⁿ⁻ʳ·bʳ
Compute specific coefficients (e.g. of x⁵)
Apply to (a−b)ⁿ and (1+x)ⁿ shortcuts
g11-mathematics-um8-t3.simple: (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b²; (a+b)³ = a³+3a²b+3ab²+b³ — the coefficients 1 3 3 1 come from PASCAL'S TRIANGLE: each row starts/ends 1, interior = sum of the two above (row 4: 1 4 6 4 1; row 5: 1 5 10 10 5 1). THE BINOMIAL THEOREM: (a+b)ⁿ = Σᵣ₌₀ⁿ nCr·aⁿ⁻ʳ·bʳ — the coefficient of the (r+1)-th term is nCr because expanding picks b from r of the n brackets (choose WHICH r — a combination!) and a from the rest. That's why combinations hide inside the algebra. GENERAL TERM: T(r+1) = nCr·aⁿ⁻ʳ·bʳ — the exam's favorite: 'find the 4th term of (2 − x)⁷' → r = 3: 7C3·2⁴·(−x)³ = 35·16·(−x³) = −560x³. Signs: (a − b)ⁿ alternates (+ − + −) because b carries a minus. (1+x)ⁿ: coefficients are just nC0…nCn — sums to 2ⁿ (set x = 1). Coefficient of xᵏ in (1+x)ⁿ is nCk — the theorem IS counting in polynomial form.
g11-mathematics-um8-t3.detailed:
The expansion engine. (a+b)ⁿ = (a+b)(a+b)···(a+b) [n factors]. A term arises by choosing b from exactly r factors and a from the other n−r: the number of ways = nCr — hence the coefficient. Powers: aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ; the exponents always sum to n; terms run r = 0 to n (n+1 terms).

Pascal's triangle. Row n holds nC0, nC1, …, nCn. Construction = the identity nCr = n−1C(r−1) + n−1Cr (case split: include or exclude the special factor). Properties: symmetry, sum 2ⁿ, alternating sum 0, diagonals = counting numbers/triangular numbers (hockey-stick).

Term-finding workflow. For 'coefficient of xᵏ in (pa + qb)ⁿ': general term nCr·(pa)ⁿ⁻ʳ·(qb)ʳ = nCr·pⁿ⁻ʳ·qʳ·aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ; match the x-exponent: solve for r, then plug. Example: coefficient of x⁵ in (x + 2)⁸: need 8−r = 5 → r = 3: 8C3·2³ = 56·8 = 448.

Substitution tricks. x = 1: (1+1)ⁿ = Σ nCr = 2ⁿ. x = −1: (1−1)ⁿ = Σ(−1)ʳnCr = 0 (even/odd subsets balance). Differentiate (1+x)ⁿ and set x = 1: Σ r·nCr = n·2ⁿ⁻¹ — the theorem as a generating function (preview of why it matters beyond expansion).

workedExamples.problem: Expand (a+b)⁴.
Find the 3rd term of (x − 2)⁶.
Coefficient of x³ in (1 + 2x)⁵?
Which term of (2x − y)⁷ contains x⁴y³?
Use the theorem: value of (1.02)⁵ to 5 decimals.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the binomial's INTERNAL coefficients when (2x) or (3y) scale terms — raise the coefficient too: (2x)³ = 8x³
Sign slips in (a − b)ⁿ — odd powers of b are negative
Off-by-one: the '4th term' has r = 3
Pascal rows mis-added (each entry = sum of the two ABOVE it)
Exponent sum ≠ n — check: aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ always totals n
Claiming (a+b)² = a²+b² (the freshman dream) — the middle term 2ab is a 2C1 choice
applications: Approximation: (1+x)ⁿ ≈ 1+nx for tiny x (physics, finance compounding)
Probability: binomial distribution (next-next unit) uses nCr weights
Combinatorics proofs: counting the same set two ways (Σ nCr = 2ⁿ)
Engineering: Taylor-style truncations of powers
g11-mathematics-um8-t3.summary: The Binomial Theorem expands (a+b)ⁿ = Σ nCr·aⁿ⁻ʳ·bʳ — coefficients are combinations because each term chooses WHICH r brackets donate b. Pascal's triangle rows the coefficients (built by nCr = n−1C(r−1)+n−1Cr). The general term T(r+1) = nCr·aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ answers 'find the coefficient of xᵏ' by matching exponents. Signs alternate in (a−b)ⁿ; substituting x = 1, −1 unlocks the 2ⁿ and alternating-sum identities; small-x truncations make it an approximation tool.

questions.q: (1+x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx works well for large x.
Find the coefficient of x² in (x + 1/x)⁶.

questions.explanation: Expanding (a+b)ⁿ multiplies n brackets; each term picks b from some r of them and a from the rest — the distinct terms with r b's correspond exactly to the r-subsets of {1…n}, numbered nCr

g11-mathematics-um8-t4.overview: Random experiments, outcomes, sample spaces, and events: the vocabulary of probability — listing spaces, counting events, and the equally-likely assumption.
objectives: Identify a random experiment and its outcomes
Write sample spaces (finite) in set notation
Define events as subsets; sure/impossible/equal events
Count outcomes with t1–t2 tools
State when 'equally likely' is justified
g11-mathematics-um8-t4.simple: A RANDOM EXPERIMENT is a process with uncertain outcome you can repeat: toss a coin, roll a die, pick a student at random. The SAMPLE SPACE S = the list of ALL possible outcomes: die → S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}; two coins → {HH, HT, TH, TT} (order matters — HT ≠ TH as outcomes!); two dice → 36 ordered pairs. An EVENT = a subset of S: 'even' = {2,4,6}; 'sum 7' = {(1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1)} — 6 of 36. Special events: S itself = CERTAIN (must happen); ∅ = IMPOSSIBLE. COMPOUND events combine: A∪B ('or'), A∩B ('and'), A′ ('not A' — the complement). EQUALLY LIKELY: symmetry, not hope — a fair die's faces are indistinguishable in mechanism, so each has weight 1/6; a biased spinner's sectors are NOT equal. Counting events uses the whole toolkit: 'at least one head in 3 tosses' = 8 − 1 (TTT) = 7 outcomes (complement counting). The probability of an event (next topic) is just (favorable outcomes)/(total outcomes) — so COUNTING the space correctly IS half the subject. Common trap: 'two dice sum to 7' vs 'sum to 2' — both look like 'one combination' but 7 has 6 paths, 2 has 1 — the space is the 36 PAIRS, not the 11 sums.
g11-mathematics-um8-t4.detailed:
Space construction. Ordered pairs/tuples when components are distinguishable (die 1 vs die 2, first coin vs second); combinations when the draw is simultaneous and order-free (two cards from a deck: 52C2 = 1326 hands). The physical process decides: with replacement → independent slots (product rule); without → shrinking (permutations/combinations).

Event algebra. Subset language: A ⊆ S; A∪B, A∩B, A′ obey the same rules as sets (De Morgan: (A∩B)′ = A′∪B′). Mutually exclusive (disjoint): A∩B = ∅ — 'die is 3 AND is even' impossible. Exhaustive: union = S — 'odd ∪ even = S'. These two words unlock the addition rule next topic.

Counting event sizes. n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B) (inclusion-exclusion from t1). 'At least one' → complement: n(A′) = n(S) − n(A). 'Exactly one' → careful case split. Sample sizes: coin n tosses → 2ⁿ; die n throws → 6ⁿ; k cards → 52Ck.

Equally-likely discipline. The classical model P = n(A)/n(S) requires every OUTCOME in S to share probability — verify by symmetry of the mechanism. 'Sum of two dice' as a 11-element space is WRONG for the classical formula (sums aren't equally likely); the 36-pair space is right (pairs are). Choose the finest symmetric space, then count inside it.

workedExamples.problem: Write S for: (a) one die, (b) two coins, (c) one die + one coin.
workedExamples.answer: Sizes 6, 4, 12 — order distinguishes HT/TH and die/coin

workedExamples.problem: Two dice: list the event 'sum = 8' and count it.
3 coins tossed: event 'at least one head' — count via complement.
Draw 2 cards without replacement: size of S?
workedExamples.answer: 1326 unordered hands (or 52·51 = 2652 ordered — consistent either way)

workedExamples.problem: A bag: 3 red, 2 blue. Draw 2. Write the space and check equal likelihood.
workedExamples.substitution: 5C2 = 10 pairs — each pair equally likely (identical draw mechanism)
workedExamples.answer: 10 equally-likely pairs; color events count inside them (e.g. RR: 3C2 = 3 → 3/10)

commonMistakes: Collapsing HT/TH into 'one head' — outcomes must be distinguishable atoms
Using sums (11 values) as the two-die space — not equally likely
Forgetting order where the process has it (first/second draw)
Assuming equal likelihood without symmetry (weighted dice, big sectors)
Double-counting 'at least one' — use complements
Mixing with/without replacement in one count
applications: Games & gambling: fair odds need correct spaces
Quality control: sampling lots = event counting
Genetics: Punnett squares are sample spaces (3:1 ratios)
Election polls: random selection = equally-likely sampling
g11-mathematics-um8-t4.summary: A random experiment has a sample space S of all outcomes — built with order where the process distinguishes it (two coins: HH, HT, TH, TT) and with combinations where it doesn't (2-card hands: 52C2). Events are subsets; combine with ∪, ∩, ′; disjoint = mutually exclusive; the whole space = certain. Classical probability needs EQUALLY LIKELY atoms — justified by mechanism symmetry, not wishful counting: use the 36-pair die space, not the 11 sums. Count event sizes with the product/combination tools and complements — then t5 divides.

questions.q: Every event is a subset of the sample space.
Sums of two dice are equally likely.
Die + coin: write S and give |S|.
Why is 'one head in two tosses' probability 1/2, not 1/3?
questions.explanation: The three 'patterns' (0, 1, 2 heads) are NOT equally likely atoms: one-head arises from two distinct outcomes HT and TH out of four — 2/4 = 1/2; collapsing atoms destroys the equal-likelihood requirement

g11-mathematics-um8-t5.overview: Probability of an event: P(A) = n(A)/n(S), the 0–1 axioms, complement rule, addition rule for disjoint and overlapping events, and multiplication for independent/sequential events.
objectives: Compute classical probabilities as favorable/total
Apply 0 ≤ P ≤ 1 and P(S) = 1
Use P(A′) = 1 − P(A)
Apply P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)
Multiply for independent and sequential events
g11-mathematics-um8-t5.simple: PROBABILITY = favorable ÷ total (when atoms are equally likely): P(even die) = 3/6 = ½. THE LAWS: (1) 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1 — impossible 0, certain 1. (2) COMPLEMENT: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) — 'at least one' problems live here: P(at least one 6 in two rolls) = 1 − (5/6)² = 11/36. (3) ADDITION: 'A or B' — if disjoint, P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B) (die: even OR >4 = 3/6+2/6−1/6... careful: {2,4,6}∪{5,6} = {2,4,5,6} = 4/6 — the overlap 6 counted twice, so subtract P(A∩B): general rule P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)). (4) MULTIPLICATION: 'A AND B' in sequence = P(A)·P(B|A); INDEPENDENT events (one doesn't shift the other): P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B) — two coins both heads = ½·½ = ¼. WITH vs WITHOUT replacement: drawing two aces without replacement: 4/52 · 3/51 (the second draw's odds SHIFTED — dependence); with replacement: (4/52)². The tree diagram: branches multiply (along), add (across cases). Read the question: OR → add (watch overlap); AND → multiply (watch dependence).
g11-mathematics-um8-t5.detailed:
Axiom frame. Kolmogorov-lite: P(S) = 1; disjoint events add. Everything else derives: P(A′) = 1 − P(A) (A, A′ partition S); general addition via A∪B = A ⊎ (B−A∩B) split; monotonicity A ⊆ B → P(A) ≤ P(B).

Conditional & independence. P(B|A) = P(A∩B)/P(A) — probability after learning A (shrink the space to A). Independent ⟺ P(B|A) = P(B) ⟺ P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B). Replacement decides: with → independent (space resets); without → dependent (counts shrink — hypergeometric flavor). 'At least one' via complement is the single most useful exam move: P = 1 − P(none)ⁿ.

Counting-division method. For equally likely atoms: P(A) = n(A)/n(S) with counts from t1–t2: e.g. 2 aces from 52: (4C2)/(52C2) = 6/1326 = 1/221 — matches the sequential product 4/52·3/51. Choose counting or tree by convenience; they must agree.

Common structures. Dice sums: count in the 36-space. Cards: sequential-without-replacement products or combination ratios. Tosses: 2ⁿ-space, complements for 'at least one'. Mutually exclusive vs independent: disjoint events with positive probability are NEVER independent (if A happens, B's probability crashed to 0 — maximal dependence) — the classic conceptual trap.

workedExamples.problem: One card: P(king OR heart)?
Two dice: P(sum = 9 OR sum > 11)?
P(at least one 6 in three rolls)?
Bag 5 red, 3 blue; draw 2 without replacement: P(both red)?
Coin + die: P(head AND a 4)?

commonMistakes: Adding overlapping events without subtracting the intersection
Multiplying disjoint-event probabilities for 'OR' (add for OR, multiply for AND)
Treating without-replacement draws as independent (odds shift!)
Forgetting the complement trick and grinding 'at least one' case-by-case
Confusing mutually exclusive with independent (they're opposites in spirit)
Wrong space: computing on collapsed outcomes (sums) instead of atoms (pairs)
applications: Insurance & risk: premium = probability × cost
Medicine: test accuracy = conditional probability (P(disease|positive))
Gaming: house edges are addition/multiplication rules in disguise
Weather: '30% chance of rain' = long-run frequency reading
g11-mathematics-um8-t5.summary: Probability assigns 0–1 weights: P(A) = n(A)/n(S) on equally likely atoms. The rulebook: complement P(A′) = 1−P(A) (the 'at least one' weapon); addition P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B) (subtract the overlap); multiplication P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B|A), which becomes P(A)P(B) for independent mechanisms. Replacement decides independence. OR → add, AND → multiply, and disjoint ≠ independent — the trap that outlives every first course.

questions.q: Two independent events P = 0.5 and 0.4: P(both):
Disjoint events with P > 0 are independent.
'At least one' is best computed via the ___ rule:
Two coins: P(at least one head)?
Explain why P(B|A) uses a shrunken sample space.
questions.explanation: Learning A occurred discards every outcome outside A — the new space is A itself, so B's share becomes n(A∩B)/n(A) = P(A∩B)/P(A): conditioning is literally re-normalizing on the reduced space

g11-mathematics-um8-t6.overview: Real-life applications of probability: expected value and fair games, risk decisions, conditional reasoning (medical tests, base rates), and probability in everyday Ethiopian contexts.
objectives: Compute expected value E = Σ x·P(x)
Judge game fairness via EV
Apply conditional probability to test accuracy
Respect base rates in risk statements
Model real situations (insurance, weather, queues)
g11-mathematics-um8-t6.simple: Probability leaves the textbook at DECISIONS. EXPECTED VALUE: the long-run average payoff — E = Σ (value × its probability). Lottery ticket: 1% chance of 1000 birr, else 0 → E = 10 birr; ticket costs 15 → EV of playing = −5: the game is unfair BY 5 per ticket (the house's cut). Insurance is the mirror: you pay a small certain loss to avoid a rare big one — the premium sits near the insurer's EV plus margin. MEDICAL TESTS — the conditional trap: a disease hits 1 in 1000; the test is 99% accurate; you test positive. P(disease|positive) ≠ 0.99! Out of 100,000 people: 100 sick (≈99 test positive) + 99,900 healthy (≈999 false positives) → true rate = 99/(99+999) ≈ 9%. The BASE RATE (1/1000) dominates — ignoring it is the prosecutor's fallacy. WEATHER: '40% rain' = in similar historical conditions it rained 40% of the time — carry the umbrella when the COST of getting wet beats the hassle. GAMES: fair ⟺ EV = 0 for all; a 'strategy' that can't beat the house edge is probability working as advertised. Queues, spare parts, exam guessing (P(correct) × marks − penalty): all EV arithmetic.
g11-mathematics-um8-t6.detailed:
EV mechanics. E(X) = Σ xᵢpᵢ over the outcome distribution. Linearity: E(aX+b) = aE(X)+b; E(X+Y) = E(X)+E(Y) (no independence needed). Fair game: E = 0. Decision rule: play if E > cost; the risk-neutral reading — real people add risk aversion (why insurance exists even when E < premium).

Bayes by counting. The clean method: imagine a concrete population (100,000), apply sensitivities/specificities as counts, read the ratio. P(D|+) = [P(+|D)·P(D)] / [P(+|D)P(D) + P(+|D′)P(D′)] — the formula, but the COUNT version beats memorization and exposes base-rate collapse: rare disease + imperfect test → mostly false positives among positives.

Risk language. '1 in 20' vs '5%' — same number, different gut reaction (frequency framing). Absolute vs relative risk (t5's misuse link): 'doubles' from 0.1% → 0.2% is +0.1 percentage points. Independence assumptions in chains: system works iff all components do → P = Πpᵢ (series); any backup suffices → 1 − Π(1−pᵢ) (parallel redundancy — spare tires, generators).

Local models. Crop insurance: payout EV = drought probability × yield loss. Mobile money fraud limits: P(loss) × size. Exam guessing: 4-option MCQ, E = ¼·1 + ¾·(−¼) = 0.0625 — barely positive; with ⅓-mark penalty E ≈ 0: pure guessing nets nothing, elimination raises it.

workedExamples.problem: Game: roll a die; 6 pays 20 birr, else nothing. Ticket 3 birr. Fair?

workedExamples.problem: Disease 1/500; test 98% sensitive, 95% specific. P(sick | positive)?

workedExamples.answer: ≈ 3.8% — positive still means probably fine (base rate!)

applications: Insurance & micro-insurance pricing (drought, livestock)
Public health: screening programs and test counseling
Engineering: redundancy design (bridges, power grids, backups)

Everyday: umbrella logic, warranty decisions, guessing strategy
g11-mathematics-um8-t6.summary: Applied probability = decisions under uncertainty. Expected value (Σ x·p) prices games, tickets, warranties — fair means EV 0; net EV subtracts the entry cost. Conditional reasoning by COUNTS on an imagined population defeats the base-rate trap: rare condition + imperfect test → positives mostly false. Series systems multiply reliabilities; parallel backups square failure away. Gambler's fallacy, conditional flips, and gross-vs-net are the three poisons — name them, avoid them, and probability becomes a decision tool rather than a trivia game.

Why do insurers happily sell EV-negative-to-them policies?
questions.explanation: Pooling many independent risks concentrates actual payouts near the expected value (law of large numbers) — the insurer's uncertainty vanishes in volume, so a premium above EV + expenses is a near-certain profit while the buyer trades a small certain loss for protection against a rare ruinous one
